reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / corneal dystrophy literature
clinicalPearls: A rare inherited endothelial dystrophy causing bilateral corneal oedema and clouding from birth or early infancy
The autosomal recessive form, linked to SLC4A11 mutations, is the recognised entity in current classification
Corneas show diffuse ground-glass oedema with marked thickening but usually without the tearing and photophobia of congenital glaucoma
Nystagmus may develop from early visual deprivation
A key differential is primary congenital glaucoma, which is distinguished by raised intraocular pressure and a large cornea
Management of significant cases is corneal transplantation, with attention to amblyopia
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy results from a primary defect of the corneal endothelium, in the recessive form due to mutations in SLC4A11 affecting a membrane transport protein important for endothelial fluid regulation. The dysfunctional endothelium cannot maintain corneal deturgescence, so fluid accumulates in the stroma from birth or infancy, producing diffuse oedema and clouding with a thickened cornea. The resulting visual deprivation early in life can cause nystagmus and amblyopia.
additionalInvestigations: Examination of corneal clarity, thickness and diameter
Intraocular pressure measurement to exclude congenital glaucoma
Assessment for nystagmus and visual development
Exclusion of metabolic and infective causes of corneal clouding
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or enlarged cornea suggesting congenital glaucoma
Systemic features suggesting a metabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: Vision depends on corneal clarity and timely management of amblyopia; corneal transplantation can restore clarity, though paediatric grafts carry higher risks and demand vigilant amblyopia treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for primary congenital glaucoma and vice versa
Overlooking a metabolic cause of corneal clouding
Delaying intervention during the critical period of visual development
management: Definitive treatment for visually significant corneal oedema is corneal transplantation, with endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK or DMEK) increasingly preferred over penetrating keratoplasty
Use topical hypertonic saline to reduce stromal oedema and temporarily improve corneal clarity in milder cases
Aggressively treat amblyopia and correct refractive error, since early visual deprivation risks amblyopia and nystagmus
Exclude and monitor for primary congenital glaucoma, which is distinguished by raised intraocular pressure and corneal enlargement
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive SLC4A11 inheritance and test at-risk relatives
Refer to a paediatric corneal specialist for graft surgery and vigilant post-transplant follow-up given the higher risks of paediatric grafts
